Too low? No, look... I mean, I really don't. It is funny you ask it exactly like that, though, because that is exactly what my sister keeps harping on. Her and that corporate doctor, they are just a broken record. They keep saying I am in some kind of immediate danger. I am just keeping myself ready for work. That is literally all this is. I am perfectly conditioned for the job. So no, doc, I do not think it is too low at all. I think it is exactly where it needs to be for me to do what I do best, and I just wish people would stop overreacting and let me get back to it.

Well, no, not underweight. I mean, when I look in the mirror... it's complicated, I guess. Because I look at myself, especially right around the middle, you know, my stomach and my waist, and I don't see someone who's wasting away. I see someone who needs to stay tight.

Every time you twist to grab a crate, every time you brace yourself to lift a pallet jack, it all comes from the center. And over the years, I've just developed this mindset, this standard for myself. If I look in that mirror and I'm not completely tight, if there's any softness or if I'm not absolutely smaller and streamlined right there around the waist... I just feel like I'm losing my edge. I feel like I'm not that same disciplined guy who can out-lift the twenty-somethings. 

It's about discipline, doc. It really is. I've always prided myself on being the hardest worker in the room, the guy who never calls out, the guy who can keep going when everyone else is taking a breather. And that discipline, it has to show physically. If I let myself get soft, if I don't look completely lean and tight in the mirror, it feels like a personal failure. It feels like I'm letting myself go, like I'm losing the one thing I've always been able to control, which is my work ethic and my physical readiness. So no, I don't see "underweight." I see a guy who is trying desperately to maintain his discipline, to stay tight and ready for the demands of the job, because if I'm not that guy, then who am I out there on the warehouse floor?

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, "afraid" is a strong word, doc, but... yeah, I guess you could say that. I mean, it's more about control and just knowing my body. Like, if I even think about eating something heavy—say, a bowl of rice, or some thick bread, or anything that's got too much grease or oil in it—my mind just starts racing. I can't stop thinking about it. I just picture that heavy food sitting right there in my gut, turning straight into fat, just weighing me down almost instantly. 

It's like this constant loop in my head. I'll eat something like that, maybe if I'm at a family thing and my sister pushes a plate in front of me, and for the rest of the night, I'm just hyper-aware of how my stomach feels. I can almost feel it expanding, you know? And then, I can't even sleep right because I'm just waiting for morning. The second I wake up, before I even have a glass of water, I have to step on the scale. I just have to know. Or I'll grab my work belt—the heavy leather one I wear on the floor—and I'll pull it tight just to check the notch. I have to make sure it still hits that exact same hole it always does. 

If it feels even a fraction of an inch tighter, or if the scale bumps up even a tiny bit, it just ruins my whole day. I feel like I've completely let myself go, like I've lost that discipline I was just talking about. Because in my line of work, you start putting on weight, you start getting sluggish, and before you know it, you're the guy they're rotating out for the younger crew. I can't let that happen. So yeah, I guess I am terrified of putting on weight, because to me, gaining weight means losing my edge, losing my job, losing everything I've built my life around. I just can't risk it for a piece of bread, you know? It's just not worth the anxiety it puts me through.

If I stand there and I don't see that I'm smaller, if I don't see that my core is completely tight-looking right across the middle... well, I don't see a guy who's "too thin," I see a guy who is slipping. I feel like if I'm not smaller and tight-looking, then I'm just not the disciplined man I used to be on the warehouse floor. And that's a hard pill to swallow, doc. Because you have to understand my history there. I started moving freight when I was twenty-two years old. Back then, I could throw eighty-pound sacks of concrete over my shoulder all day and still have the energy to go out after. Now I'm fifty-five. The only thing separating me from the guys who got washed out, the guys who blew out their backs or just couldn't keep up the pace and got let go, is my absolute discipline. 

So when I look in that mirror, I'm looking for proof that I still have it. If my waist looks even a little bit soft, or if I don't look as small and compact as I need to be to maneuver around those pallets, my mind just goes straight to, "You're losing it. You're getting sloppy." It's not about seeing some distorted fun-house mirror thing, it's about seeing the truth of my work ethic. If I don't look small and tight, I just feel like a fraud. I feel like I'm turning into one of those guys who has to ask the younger crew for help lifting a crate, and I will absolutely not be that guy. I refuse. So I guess I don't see "weight," doc. I see my discipline, and I have to make sure it's still there every single day.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, restrict... I mean, I guess that’s one word for it, doc. It just goes right back to what I was saying about the discipline and not getting sluggish. Listen, when you're working a twelve-hour shift moving pallets, you don't have time to be bogged down by a heavy stomach anyway. You just don't. I see these young guys, these kids really, they come into the breakroom with these massive fast-food bags, eating burgers and fries, and then they're dragging their feet for the next four hours. They're sweating, they're slow, they're complaining about their backs. I can't do that. I absolutely refuse to be that guy. 

So, yeah, I keep things very, very controlled. Most days, honestly, I just keep it to black coffee. I'll bring a big thermos of it and that just keeps the engine running, you know? It gives me the energy without the weight. Maybe, if I really feel like I need something solid to get through the last few hours, I'll have a boiled egg, or maybe just a little bit of tuna out of a can. It's clean, it's light, and most importantly, it doesn't sit in my gut and make me feel like I'm expanding and getting soft. 

And the thing is, if I have a day off—which isn't often, because I pick up the overtime whenever they offer it, I like to stay busy—but if I'm at home and I'm not actually out there moving freight on a shift, well... my mind just starts rationalizing it. I tell myself I don’t need a real meal anyway. It just doesn't make sense to put fuel in the tank if the truck isn't moving, right? Because if I sit down and eat a full meal on a day off, that's when that anxiety really kicks into overdrive. That's when I feel like I'm just sitting in my recliner letting the food turn straight into fat, just completely ruining all that hard work and discipline I've built up all week. So I just don't do it. I stick to the coffee, I stick to the bare minimum, because the alternative—feeling that softness, feeling like I'm losing control—is just something I can't live with.

I mean, I really don't. It is funny you ask it exactly like that, though, because that is exactly what my sister keeps harping on. Her and that corporate doctor, they are just a broken record. They keep saying I am in some kind of immediate danger. My sister called me just the other night, practically in tears, going on and on about how she is worried sick, how my weight is dangerously low and she thinks I am going to collapse or something. And then this doctor at the clearance clinic pulls the exact same routine, acting like I am about to drop dead right there on his linoleum floor. \n\nBut they are just making it so much bigger than it actually is. They are blowing the whole thing way out of proportion because, honestly, neither of them has a clue what my day-to-day life actually requires. My sister sits at a computer all day, and that doctor, well, he just sits in an exam room checking boxes. They do not understand the mechanics of moving freight for a living. I have tried to explain it to them, I really have. I tell them, look, I am just keeping myself light. I am keeping myself sharp. When you are out there on the warehouse floor, dodging forklifts, swinging heavy boxes onto pallets for twelve hours, you need to be agile. If you have extra weight on your frame, it just slows your reaction time down, it wears out your knees and your back faster... it is just basic physics, right? \n\nI am just keeping myself ready for work. That is literally all this is. I am perfectly conditioned for the job. But they just look at some standard medical chart on a wall and decide I am in danger, completely ignoring the fact that I am out-working guys half my age every single shift. So no, doc, I do not think it is too low at all. I think it is exactly where it needs to be for me to do what I do best, and I just wish people would stop overreacting and let me get back to it.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you look underweight when you look in the mirror?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not underweight. I mean, when I look in the mirror... it's complicated, I guess. I see someone who needs to stay tight. \n\nIt's like this... when you're on the floor for a twelve-hour shift, your core is everything. Every time you twist to grab a crate, every time you brace yourself to lift a pallet jack, it all comes from the center. If I look in that mirror and I'm not completely tight, if there's any softness or if I'm not absolutely smaller and streamlined right there around the waist... I just feel like I'm losing my edge. I feel like I'm not that same disciplined guy who can out-lift the twenty-somethings. \n\nIt's about discipline, doc. It really is. I've always prided myself on being the hardest worker in the room, the guy who never calls out, the guy who can keep going when everyone else is taking a breather. And that discipline, it has to show physically. If I let myself get soft, if I don't look completely lean and tight in the mirror, it feels like a personal failure. It feels like I'm letting myself go, like I'm losing the one thing I've always been able to control, which is my work ethic and my physical readiness. So no, I don't see \"underweight.\" I see a guy who is trying desperately to maintain his discipline, to stay tight and ready for the demands of the job, because if I'm not that guy, then who am I out there on the warehouse floor?\n\nDoctor: Are you afraid of gaining weight?\n\nPatient: Well, \"afraid\" is a strong word, doc, but... yeah, I guess you could say that. I feel like if I'm not smaller and tight-looking, then I'm just not the disciplined man I used to be on the warehouse floor. And that's a hard pill to swallow, doc. Because you have to understand my history there. I started moving freight when I was twenty-two years old. Back then, I could throw eighty-pound sacks of concrete over my shoulder all day and still have the energy to go out after. Now I'm fifty-five. The only thing separating me from the guys who got washed out, the guys who blew out their backs or just couldn't keep up the pace and got let go, is my absolute discipline. \n\nSo when I look in that mirror, I'm looking for proof that I still have it. If my waist looks even a little bit soft, or if I don't look as small and compact as I need to be to maneuver around those pallets, my mind just goes straight to, \"You're losing it. You're getting sloppy.\" It's not about seeing some distorted fun-house mirror thing, it's about seeing the truth of my work ethic. If I don't look small and tight, I just feel like a fraud. I feel like I'm turning into one of those guys who has to ask the younger crew for help lifting a crate, and I will absolutely not be that guy. I refuse. So I guess I don't see \"weight,\" doc. I see these young guys, these kids really, they come into the breakroom with these massive fast-food bags, eating burgers and fries, and then they're dragging their feet for the next four hours. Well, yeah, I avoid them like the plague now. I really do. Because you go to these things—like, the guys from the loading dock, they like to do these Friday night get-togethers, maybe head down to the pub near the rail yard, or somebody hosts a barbecue at their place. And it’s always just a mountain of the worst possible stuff. It’s all heavy carbs and fried junk. 

And the thing is, doc, I just can't handle being around that kind of food anymore, let alone eating it. If I go, they're going to push it on me. "Hey, grab a plate, have a bun, eat some of this." But if I cave... if I eat rice, or bread, or something greasy like those wings or burgers they always order, it just completely derails my mind. I can’t stop thinking it will sit on me right away. I mean that literally. I'll be sitting there in a folding chair, trying to make small talk about the forklift maintenance schedule or whatever, but my brain is just screaming at me. I can actually feel the grease and the bread just... expanding in my gut, turning into dead weight, just sitting there attaching itself to my waistline while I'm still at the party. 

It completely ruins the night, and then it ruins the next day, too. Because I'll go home, I'll toss and turn, and the next morning, the very first thing I have to do—before I even think about brewing that pot of coffee I told you about—is I have to check. I'll step right on the scale, and then I'll pull on my work pants and pull my belt tight, right to the notch I always use. I'll check the scale or my belt the next morning to make absolutely sure I didn’t let myself go. If that belt feels even a fraction of a millimeter tighter, or if the number on that scale blinks even a point higher, I feel like a total failure. I feel like I've just thrown away years of discipline for a stupid piece of bread. 

So, it's just not worth it. I tell the guys I'm busy. I tell them I've got chores, or I'm trying to catch some sleep before an early shift. I make up whatever excuse I need to. Because the mental torture of eating that greasy stuff and then waking up in a panic, yanking at my belt loops to prove to myself I'm not getting soft... it's just too much, doc. It's so much easier to just stay home and keep the engine running clean.

Quality of life... you know, it’s funny you phrase it exactly like that, doc, because I was just thinking about this the other day while I was out on my morning walk. What really makes a good quality of life? To me, it's independence. It's capability. It's knowing that your engine is running clean and you don't have to rely on anybody else to get the job done.

I feel like I'm turning into one of those guys who has to ask the younger crew for help lifting a crate, and I will absolutely not be that guy. I refuse. So I guess I don't see \"weight,\" doc. I see my discipline, and I have to make sure it's still there every single day.\n\nDoctor: Do you restrict what you eat because you're afraid of gaining weight?\n\nPatient: Well, restrict... I mean, I guess that’s one word for it, doc. It just goes right back to what I was saying about the discipline and not getting sluggish. Listen, when you're working a twelve-hour shift moving pallets, you don't have time to be bogged down by a heavy stomach anyway. You just don't. I see these young guys, these kids really, they come into the breakroom with these massive fast-food bags, eating burgers and fries, and then they're dragging their feet for the next four hours. They're sweating, they're slow, they're complaining about their backs. I can't do that. I absolutely refuse to be that guy. \n\nSo, yeah, I keep things very, very controlled. Most days, honestly, I just keep it to black coffee. I'll bring a big thermos of it and that just keeps the engine running, you know? It gives me the energy without the weight. Maybe, if I really feel like I need something solid to get through the last few hours, I'll have a boiled egg, or maybe just a little bit of tuna out of a can. It's clean, it's light, and most importantly, it doesn't sit in my gut and make me feel like I'm expanding and getting soft. \n\nAnd the thing is, if I have a day off—which isn't often, because I pick up the overtime whenever they offer it, I like to stay busy—but if I'm at home and I'm not actually out there moving freight on a shift, well... my mind just starts rationalizing it. I tell myself I don’t need a real meal anyway. It just doesn't make sense to put fuel in the tank if the truck isn't moving, right? Because if I sit down and eat a full meal on a day off, that's when that anxiety really kicks into overdrive. That's when I feel like I'm just sitting in my recliner letting the food turn straight into fat, just completely ruining all that hard work and discipline I've built up all week. So I just don't do it. I stick to the coffee, I stick to the bare minimum, because the alternative—feeling that softness, feeling like I'm losing control—is just something I can't live with.\n\nDoctor: Does your fear of gaining weight affect what you eat or do on days when you're not working?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, like I... like I was just saying a minute ago, doc, it absolutely does. Honestly, the days off are almost harder than the days I'm on the floor. Because when I'm at the warehouse, I have a rhythm, you know? I have the pallets, the schedule, the sweat, the constant motion. But on a Sunday, if I don't pick up an overtime shift—which, like I said, I try to do just to avoid this exact situation—but if I'm stuck at home, that fear just kind of takes over everything. \n\nI mean, I know I just told you that most days I keep it to black coffee, maybe a boiled egg or a little tuna. But when I'm at home and I'm not moving freight on a shift, I just completely lock it down. I tell myself I don't need a real meal anyway. And I really believe that. I mean, why would I? It's just basic mechanics to me. If your truck is parked in the driveway, you don't keep pumping gas into it, right? It'll just overflow. And that's exactly how I picture my body. \n\nIf I'm just sitting in my living room, maybe trying to watch a game or read the paper, and I even think about eating something substantial, I can literally feel the panic rising up in my chest. I start thinking about how I'm not burning it off. I think about how every single bite is just going to settle right around my waistline and make me soft. So I just stick to the coffee. I'll brew a whole pot in the morning and just nurse it all day long. Sometimes I'll catch myself pacing around the house, doing yard work I don't even need to do, fixing hinges that aren't even squeaking, just to keep moving. Because if I sit still, my mind starts telling me I'm getting lazy, that I'm losing my edge, that I'm putting on weight just by sitting in the recliner. \n\nSo, yeah, my days off are completely dictated by it. I just don't eat a real meal on those days, period. It's just not worth the mental gymnastics I have to go through if I do. It's so much easier to just feel empty than to sit there feeling... heavy. You know what I mean? It's just about keeping the discipline tight, even when nobody is watching. Especially when nobody is watching.\n\nDoctor: Has your fear of gaining weight ever caused you to avoid social gatherings or events where food is involved?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, I avoid them like the plague now. I really do. I feel like I've just thrown away years of discipline for a stupid piece of bread. \n\nSo, it's just not worth it. I tell the guys I'm busy. I tell them I've got chores, or I'm trying to catch some sleep before an early shift. I make up whatever excuse I need to. It's so much easier to just stay home and keep the engine running clean.\n\nDoctor: Have you avoided any important life events or activities because of your concerns about weight?\n\nPatient: Well, avoided? Well, I mean... I guess there's a difference, sure. But I don't think it's because I'm seeing things wrong. I think it's because they just don't get what I'm doing. 

Like my sister, right? We talked about her. She looks at me and she just sees... I don't know, she sees something to panic about. She tells me I look like a skeleton, that I'm wasting away, that I'm in some kind of immediate danger. And that clinic doctor, the one who refused to sign my clearance form so I could start the new logistics job—he's the exact same way. He took one look at the scale, looked at me, and started talking about how my BMI was dangerously low and how I was putting my heart at risk. He actually used the word "severe." He said I was in a state of severe malnutrition. 

But I look in the mirror, doc, and I just see a guy who is ready to work. I see a guy who doesn't have a gut hanging over his belt like the rest of the guys at the warehouse. I see someone who is lean, who is sharp, who has stripped away all the excess baggage so the engine can run clean. 

They keep saying I'm in danger, but they're just making it so much bigger than it actually is. They're projecting their own ideas of what a fifty-five-year-old man should look like onto me. They think because I don't look soft and bloated like every other guy my age, there must be a medical emergency. But I'm just keeping myself light. I have to be light to move fast on the floor. I have to be sharp to route the trucks and manage the dock schedule. If I carried around an extra twenty or thirty pounds like they want me to, I'd be sluggish. I'd be slow. I'd be just like those guys complaining about their knees every morning. 

So, yeah, what they see and what I see are different. But it's not because I'm blind to my own weight. I know I'm thin. I work very hard to be thin. It's just that they don't understand the purpose of it. They don't understand that this is exactly where I need to be to do my job and live my life the way I want to. They're just blowing the whole thing completely out of proportion.

Fear of gaining weight... well, I don't know if I'd use the word "fear," doc. It's more about being strictly vigilant. But, I mean, I guess it does get in my head a bit. So, if that's what you mean by affecting how I perceive my weight, then sure, I guess it does.
